questions.question: What is the blank identifier (`_`) in Go, and what does it do?
questions.title: Go's blank identifier: meaning and behaviour
questions.direct_answer: The blank identifier is written as `_`. It receives a value and immediately discards it, which lets Go code intentionally ignore a return value or one value produced by `range`. `_` is not a normal variable: its value cannot be read later. It should communicate that a value is deliberately unused, not hide information the program should handle.

sections.title: Interview answer

beats.cue: Define the underscore by what happens to its value
beats.spokenText: Go's blank identifier is written as `_`. It can receive a value in a declaration or assignment, but that value is discarded instead of being stored in a variable the program can read later. Each use of `_` simply says, “this position is intentionally unused.”

beats.cue: Separate it from an ordinary variable binding
beats.spokenText: The blank identifier is not a variable named underscore. Code cannot print it, compare it, take its address, or retrieve an earlier value from it. It also does not count as a newly declared variable in a short declaration. The right-hand expression still runs; only the selected result is thrown away.

beats.cue: Show the ordinary multi-value and range uses
beats.spokenText: The common uses come from Go syntax that produces more than one value. In `width, _ := dimensions()`, the width is kept and the height is intentionally ignored. In `for _, name := range names`, the loop keeps each name and discards the index.

beats.cue: Distinguish the two specialised underscore forms
beats.spokenText: Two specialised forms use the same spelling for a different purpose. A blank import such as `_ "database/sql/driver"` imports a package only for initialization side effects. An assertion such as `var _ io.Reader = (*File)(nil)` asks the compiler to verify that `*File` implements `io.Reader`.

beats.cue: Finish with the information-safety boundary
beats.spokenText: The blank identifier is safe only when the discarded information truly cannot affect correctness. An error normally changes what the caller should do, so `value, err := strconv.Atoi(input)` should keep and check `err`. Using `value, _` merely to make code compile can turn invalid input into a believable zero value.
beats.recallRule: Use the blank identifier for a deliberately irrelevant result, never as storage and never as a shortcut for handling important information.

sections.content:
Go's blank identifier is written as `_`. It can receive a value in a declaration or assignment, but that value is discarded instead of being stored in a variable the program can read later. Each use of `_` simply says, “this position is intentionally unused.”

The blank identifier is not a variable named underscore. Code cannot print it, compare it, take its address, or retrieve an earlier value from it. It also does not count as a newly declared variable in a short declaration. The right-hand expression still runs; only the selected result is thrown away.

The common uses come from Go syntax that produces more than one value. In `width, _ := dimensions()`, the width is kept and the height is intentionally ignored. In `for _, name := range names`, the loop keeps each name and discards the index.

Two specialised forms use the same spelling for a different purpose. A blank import such as `_ "database/sql/driver"` imports a package only for initialization side effects. An assertion such as `var _ io.Reader = (*File)(nil)` asks the compiler to verify that `*File` implements `io.Reader`.

The blank identifier is safe only when the discarded information truly cannot affect correctness. An error normally changes what the caller should do, so `value, err := strconv.Atoi(input)` should keep and check `err`. Using `value, _` merely to make code compile can turn invalid input into a believable zero value.

sections.title: What the blank identifier changes
sections.content:
The blank identifier can appear wherever Go needs an identifier on the left side of a declaration or assignment. The right-hand expression is still evaluated, but the result placed in `_` is not stored in an addressable binding. Every underscore occurrence is independent, so there is no previous blank value to retrieve.

This matters in short declarations: `_` never counts as a newly declared variable. It is useful for selecting one result from a multi-value operation or one part of a range iteration, but it should describe an intentional information choice rather than silence Go's unused-variable checks.

Blank imports and compile-time interface assertions are specialised forms. The import keeps initialization side effects without a package binding; the assertion asks the compiler to check assignability without creating a runtime object for later use.

sections.title: Small Go example
When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Use `_` for an unneeded range index or value, for an intentionally ignored return value only when failure is impossible or irrelevant, and for compile-time interface assertions such as `var _ io.Reader = (*File)(nil)`. A named variable preserves information and should be used when the value affects correctness, logging, or debugging. `_` is better only when retaining that value would add no meaning and the discard is deliberate.

beats.cue: Start with the selection rule rather than a syntax list
beats.spokenText: Use `_` when Go requires a result position but that particular result has no meaning for the current operation. The decision is about information: if losing the value cannot change correctness, diagnosis, logging, or later work, an explicit discard can make the code clearer.

beats.cue: Show how range syntax changes with the needed part
beats.spokenText: For a range loop, keep only the part the loop needs. Use `for i := range items` when only the index matters, and `for _, item := range items` when only the value matters. Name both values when both position and data help the work.

sections.content:
Use `_` when Go requires a result position but that particular result has no meaning for the current operation. The decision is about information: if losing the value cannot change correctness, diagnosis, logging, or later work, an explicit discard can make the code clearer.

For a range loop, keep only the part the loop needs. Use `for i := range items` when only the index matters, and `for _, item := range items` when only the value matters. Name both values when both position and data help the work.

A map lookup can return `value, ok`. If the question is only whether the key exists, `_, ok := scores[name]` keeps the Boolean and deliberately drops the stored score. The result being discarded is safe because the operation never intends to use that score.

Do not apply the same rule blindly to an `error`. In `n, err := strconv.Atoi(input)`, invalid text produces both a zero integer and a non-nil error. If the program needs to distinguish invalid input from the valid number zero, the error must remain named and checked.

Use a blank import only when package initialization is the intended feature, and usually document why that hidden startup work is needed. Use `var _ Interface = (*Type)(nil)` when a compile-time interface assertion protects a design contract. In every other case, name the result when future readers may need to understand or act on it.

sections.title: When the blank identifier is appropriate
sections.content:
Start with the results the operation needs to keep. A value-only range loop needs the element but not its index, so `for _, value := range values` is a natural discard. An existence-only map lookup needs `ok` but not the stored value, so `_, ok := mapping[key]` states that question directly.

Keep a named result when it controls success, failure, logging, cleanup, or a later calculation. Errors usually belong in this group because the other returned value may be a zero or partial result on failure.

Prefer omission when Go syntax supports it, such as `for index := range values` for an index-only loop. Reserve blank imports for required initialization side effects and blank interface assertions for deliberate compile-time contract checks.

sections.title: Discarding is an information decision
sections.content:
A named variable creates a binding that can be inspected and used later. The blank identifier accepts the same assignment position but removes that result from the program immediately. The function call and its side effects still happen, so `_` changes retained information rather than execution of the right-hand side.

For a map lookup, `_, ok := values[key]` is precise when only existence matters. For parsing, `n, err := strconv.Atoi(input)` should normally keep both values because the error decides whether `n` is trustworthy.

Go's unused-local rule is not a reason to discard useful information. Choose `_` after deciding the value is irrelevant; otherwise name the result and make its handling visible.
